knowledge_point.title: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Using a Diagram

questions.:question/problem:
![](images/48/48517c5d3fa340bed1cc7b5493f0099a72afa79d9e0690b79695afe018c8a05c.png)

The diagram above shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. If the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $(6,\frac{\pi }{6})$ and $m∠AOB=\frac{\pi }{2},$ what are the Cartesian coordinates of $B?$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(6,\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we must have $r=6.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $6,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $6.$ 

Notice that one must traverse the circle counterclockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta $-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{\pi }{6},$ the $\theta $-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}=\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(6,\frac{2\pi }{3})$ 

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =6\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =6\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =3\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-3,3\sqrt{3}).$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

exemplars.:question/problem:
![](images/1c/1ca3b41e82afa7c9a6dd513ecc900fc41ec08432027f4fa692836299bf5c3540.png)

The diagram shows $A$ and $B$ on a circle centered at the origin $O$. Point $A$ has polar coordinates $(6,30^\circ)$ and $\angle AOB=30^\circ$.

Moving from $A$ to $B$ along the marked arc is counterclockwise, so add the marked angle to the angle of $A$. Use $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$ to find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$.

Which ordered pair is correct?
exemplars.:question/worked-solution:
Both points lie on the same circle, so the radius for $B$ is $r=6$. The marked counterclockwise turn increases the polar angle:

$$
\theta_B=30^\circ+30^\circ=60^\circ.
$$

Thus $B$ has polar coordinates $(6,60^\circ)$. Convert each coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=6\cos60^\circ=6\left(\frac12\right)=3,\\
y&=6\sin60^\circ=6\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=3\sqrt3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(3,3\sqrt3)$. Both coordinates are positive, as the diagram requires.

exemplars.:question/problem:
![](images/ef/ef353618883e0fa610a179cb3103e9a59cf7bff8f6147317cf65f45bb868b6e6.png)

The diagram shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin $O$. The polar coordinates of $A$ are $(6,150^\circ)$ and $\angle AOB=30^\circ$. Use the marked arc and the positions of $A$ and $B$ to determine whether the angle of $B$ is greater or less than the angle of $A$.

What are the Cartesian coordinates of $B$?
exemplars.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ and $B$ lie on the same circle, $B$ also has radius $6$. The marked arc runs clockwise from $A$ toward $B$, so subtract the included angle:

$$
\theta_B=150^\circ-30^\circ=120^\circ.
$$

Thus the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(6,120^\circ)$. Using $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=6\cos120^\circ=6\left(-\frac12\right)=-3,\\
y&=6\sin120^\circ=6\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=3\sqrt3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $B=(-3,3\sqrt3)$. The signs agree with its position in quadrant II. The angle $30^\circ$ is the turn between the two radii, not the polar angle of $B$.

![](images/c4/c450bcb722f49ed4300043f18bc5f8b61c44d25b91312974df4ef8884d9dd8d4.png)

The diagram shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin $O$. If the polar coordinates of $A$ are $\left(6,\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ and the marked angle is $\angle AOB=\frac{7\pi}{12}$, determine the exact Cartesian coordinates of $B$.

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$.
exemplars.:question/worked-solution:
The two points lie on the same circle, so the radius for $B$ is $6$. Along the marked arc, moving from $A$ to $B$ is clockwise. Subtract the marked angle, using a common denominator:

$$
\theta_B=\frac{5\pi}{6}-\frac{7\pi}{12}
=\frac{10\pi}{12}-\frac{7\pi}{12}
=\frac{3\pi}{12}=\frac\pi4.
$$

The polar coordinates of $B$ are therefore $\left(6,\frac\pi4\right)$. Convert using $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=6\cos\left(\frac\pi4\right)=6\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)=3\sqrt2,\\
y&=6\sin\left(\frac\pi4\right)=6\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)=3\sqrt2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $B=(3\sqrt2,3\sqrt2)$. Its equal positive coordinates agree with the point on the first-quadrant diagonal.
